title: BERA Misrepresented COPE Guidelines in Retraction Statement
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Vainker makes a precise technical case that the British Educational Research Association's retraction statement made two verifiably false claims about the COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) guidelines governing when a paper should be retracted. BERA's statement claimed that undisclosed AI use does not always indicate fraud or manipulation, and that the COPE guidelines require multiple signals rather than treating undisclosed AI alone as sufficient grounds for retraction. Vainker quotes the actual COPE guidelines, which state exactly the opposite: that 'any form of misrepresentation, for example, undisclosed use of artificial intelligence' is itself a sufficient and specific ground for retraction. Undisclosed AI use is classified by COPE as a form of misrepresentation equivalent to fraud — not a signal requiring corroboration from other evidence. BERA's error is therefore not ambiguous or interpretive; it is a direct factual misstatement of a specific, quotable standard. Vainker situates this misrepresentation in a broader institutional critique: AI has hit academic institutions at their weak point, which is that organizations historically valued for intellectual rigor have been hollowed out by hyper-management, short-term metric-gaming, and a drift from their foundational purpose. BERA, he argues, no longer focuses on improving education in the UK but on irrelevant research that serves internal citation metrics — meaning that when AI slop enters its journals at scale, the institutional immune response is driven by self-protection rather than integrity. The piece signals a forthcoming follow-up presenting ten BERJ papers that BERA claims retain its confidence but contain impossible methods and citation errors.
points: BERA's retraction statement is not merely inadequate but demonstrably false: the COPE guidelines it cited actually state the reverse of BERA's characterization, classifying undisclosed AI use as a specific form of misrepresentation that is itself sufficient grounds for retraction without requiring additional corroborating signals.

The broader institutional failure Vainker diagnoses is structural: AI has exposed that academic organizations whose prestige historically rested on intellectual rigor have been hollowed out by metric-gaming management culture, leaving them without the institutional immune response needed to defend integrity when it matters.

BERA's stated position — that it retains confidence in papers containing undisclosed AI use where that use 'does not require disclosure' — is also wrong, as Vainker has documented separately; the COPE guidelines make no such exception for any category of undisclosed AI use.

The scandal of mass-publishing AI slop in a major educational research journal is made worse, not better, by a retraction response that misrepresents the governing ethical standards — it signals that the leadership class's priority is organizational face-saving rather than research integrity.

The institutional pattern Vainker identifies is self-reinforcing: organizations that publish abstruse, irrelevant research optimized for internal metrics rather than educational impact have no external accountability mechanism that would force them to take integrity failures seriously.
quotes: AI has really hit academic institutions on their weak spot — while they have historically gained their prestige through intellectual rigour and integrity, today they are hyper-managed, hollowed out organisations whose vision is narrowed to gaming short-term metrics. And so AI cheating is tolerated to the extent that it causes no immediate harm to the organisation.

In the case of the British Educational Research Association, they have long forgotten their ultimate purpose — to improve education in the UK. Instead, they publish abstruse, irrelevant research that only impacts internal academic metrics such as citation counts and diversity of authors. Without the focus on rigour and purpose, it's no surprise that they have drifted towards publishing AI slop on a mass scale.

The following paragraph makes two very confident claims about the COPE retraction guidelines, both of which are entirely and unequivocally wrong: 'In addition, undisclosed AI use does not always indicate fraud or manipulation; however, when combined with other signals, it can indicate that a paper needs further examination.'

The only mention of AI in the COPE retraction guidelines completely contradicts the above characterisation: 'Editors can decide to retract a publication if they no longer have confidence in the results and conclusions reported in the paper. Reasons for this loss of confidence can be, but are not limited to: …Any form of misrepresentation, for example…undisclosed use of artificial intelligence.'
So, in short, undisclosed use of AI is tantamount to fraud ('misrepresentation') and is itself sufficient grounds to retract the paper. BERA's incompetence and complacency truly know no bounds.

It is ridiculous that BERA is attempting to brush off this scandal of mass-publishing AI slop, and it cannot be allowed to do so. I repeat, we need education academics, but we can't allow an incompetent and complacent leadership class to disfigure educational research.
